procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 16.05.2017 passed by the Allahabad High Court in CRLR No. 1564 of 2017.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court quashed the Trial Court's Order dated 15.03.2017 (which had dismissed an application under Section 319 Cr.P.C. to summon the appellant as an additional accused) and remanded the matter back to the Trial Court for fresh examination. This was done in response to a Criminal Revision Petition filed by respondent No. 2.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (the person sought to be summoned as an additional accused) challenged the High Court's order dated 16.05.2017 before the Supreme Court, arguing that the High Court should have considered the evidence itself instead of remanding the matter. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and dismissed the application to summon the appellant as an additional accused.

directions: The impugned order passed by the High Court is set aside.
The application filed by the complainant for summoning the appellant as an additional accused is dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether the power under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. should be exercised to summon the appellant as an additional accused.

facts: An employee of the appellant was murdered, and an FIR was initially registered against unknown persons.
After investigation, police filed a chargesheet against two other individuals, listing the appellant as a prosecution witness (PW-6).
During the trial, after the appellant and other witnesses testified, the complainant filed an application under Section 319 Cr.P.C. to summon the appellant as an additional accused.
The Trial Court dismissed this application.
The High Court quashed the Trial Court's order and remanded the matter for fresh consideration.
Subsequently, the two accused who were originally charged were acquitted.
law: The power to summon an additional accused under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. is a discretionary and extraordinary power.
It must be exercised sparingly and not in a casual or cavalier manner.
The standard for summoning is higher than a prima facie case; there must be strong and cogent evidence that could likely lead to a conviction.
application: The Court examined the evidence on record and found that it did not go beyond mere suspicion against the appellant.
It noted that there was no eyewitness to the crime and that the allegations against the appellant were based on vague oral statements from other witnesses.

The Court determined that this material was not sufficient to meet the high threshold of "strong and cogent evidence" required to establish the appellant's complicity and justify summoning him under Section 319.
The Court also considered the fact that the other accused in the case had already been acquitted, which further weakened the case for adding a new accused.

Additionally, the Court criticized the High Court for remanding the matter, stating that it would only prolong the litigation and that the High Court should have decided the issue itself based on the available material.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the evidence on record was insufficient to summon the appellant as an additional accused. The material only raised a suspicion and did not meet the legal standard of strong and cogent evidence required under Section 319 Cr.P.C. Therefore, the Court allowed the appeal, set aside the High Court's order, and dismissed the application to summon the appellant.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in remanding the matter back to the Trial Court for fresh examination instead of deciding the application on its merits.

facts: An application was filed in the Trial Court under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. to summon the appellant as an additional accused.
The Trial Court dismissed this application.
On revision, the High Court quashed the Trial Court's order and remanded the matter back for a fresh examination, stating that the reasons given by the Trial Court were not sufficient.
The appellant challenged the High Court's remand order before the Supreme Court.
law: The power to summon an additional accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C. cannot be exercised on mere suspicion.
This power should only be used when there is strong and cogent evidence that could lead to a conviction.
The High Court, in its revisional power, can correct errors made by a lower court.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court's decision to remand the case was improper and would only result in prolonging the litigation.
It reasoned that the High Court had all the necessary material and evidence on record to decide the application on its merits.
Instead of remanding, the proper exercise of power would have been for the High Court to consider the evidence itself and determine if a case was made out for summoning the appellant.
The Supreme Court noted that even if the Trial Court's reasoning was 'not happily worded', the High Court could have corrected this error itself rather than sending the case back.

Furthermore, the Court observed that the other accused in the case had already been acquitted, and the evidence against the appellant did not go beyond mere suspicion, which was insufficient to meet the high standard required by Section 319 Cr.P.C.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in remanding the matter. The High Court should have decided the application on its merits to avoid unnecessary delay. Consequently, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and dismissed the application to summon the appellant as an additional accused.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the power under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C. should be exercised to summon the appellant as an additional accused.
appellant_arguments: The power to summon an additional accused under Section 319 Cr.P.C. cannot be exercised in a casual or cavalier manner and requires strong and cogent evidence that could lead to conviction, not mere suspicion.
The application to summon the appellant was filed very late, when the trial was about to conclude and all evidence had been led.
The evidence produced by the prosecution to summon the appellant was sketchy.
The other accused, against whom the chargesheet was filed, were ultimately acquitted, indicating the weakness of the prosecution's case.
The material on record was insufficient to establish the appellant's complicity in the crime as per the standards laid down by the Supreme Court.
respondent_arguments: A clear case was made out against the appellant for summoning him as an additional accused.
The trial court failed to exercise the jurisdiction vested in it.
The material already on record was sufficient to summon the appellant, and had it been considered, the appellant would have faced trial.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in remanding the matter back to the Trial Court for fresh examination instead of deciding the application on its merits.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's approach of remanding the matter for fresh examination was incorrect.
The High Court should have appreciated the available evidence itself to determine if a case was made out for summoning the appellant.
Remanding the matter only results in prolonging the litigation.
Even if the trial court's reasoning was flawed, the High Court could have corrected the error itself in the exercise of its revisional power instead of remanding the case.
respondent_arguments: The trial court had failed to exercise its jurisdiction, and while the High Court could have corrected it, it chose to remand the matter back.

cases.case_name: Hardeep Singh and Ors. v. State of Punjab & Ors.
cases.principle: For the settled principles of law regarding the exercise of jurisdiction under Section 319 of the Cr.P.C.

cases.case_name: Sagar v. State of U.P. and Anr.
cases.principle: The power under Section 319 of the Code is a discretionary and extraordinary power to be exercised sparingly. The test for summoning an additional accused is more than a prima facie case (as required for framing charges) but short of a satisfaction that the evidence, if unrebutted, would lead to conviction.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: The test for exercising the power under Section 319 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to summon an additional accused requires a standard of evidence that is more than a prima facie case as used for framing a charge, but short of the satisfaction that the evidence, if unrebutted, would lead to a conviction.
obiter: The power under Section 319 of the Code is a discretionary and extraordinary power which should be exercised sparingly and only where the circumstances of the case so warrant.
To summon an additional accused, a prima facie case can be established from evidence that has not necessarily been tested by cross-examination.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that since the evidence on record was insufficient to even secure a conviction against the accused who were originally charged and subsequently acquitted, it failed to meet the high standard required to summon the appellant as an additional accused. The acquittal of the co-accused demonstrated that the material was not strong enough to satisfy the 'more than prima facie' test for exercising power under Section 319 Cr.P.C.
legal_tests_applied: The power under Section 319 of the Code is a discretionary and extraordinary power which should be exercised sparingly and only in those cases where the circumstances of the case so warrant.

The crucial test to be applied is one which is more that prima facie case as exercised at the time of framing of charge, but short of satisfaction to an extent that the evidence, if goes unrebutted, would lead to conviction.
To summon an additional accused requires much strong evidence that near probability of his complicity.
policy_considerations: The power under Section 319 of the Code is an extraordinary power that must be exercised with caution to prevent individuals from being casually implicated in criminal proceedings without substantial evidence.
